title: Spain's Borja Iglesias Will 'Reluctantly' Shake Trump's Hand at World Cup Final to Avoid Prison
excerpt: The outspoken striker says he would 'love to do many things' but will play it safe when Trump presents the trophy at today's Argentina vs Spain final at MetLife Stadium.
body:
• Spain striker Borja Iglesias says he will shake Donald Trump's hand at today's World Cup Final but only "to avoid prison."
  • Trump is expected to present the Jules Rimet trophy at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, where Argentina face Spain.
  • Teammate Marc Cucurella recalled a previous encounter with Trump at the Club World Cup, saying he was "absolutely terrified" when the president refused to leave the stage.
  • The final marks Trump's second consecutive appearance presenting a FIFA trophy to players on US soil.

Hours before the biggest match in football, one of Spain's most politically outspoken players has made his feelings about the trophy presentation clear.

Borja Iglesias, the 33-year-old striker who has previously backed pro-Palestine protesters, painted his nails black for Black Lives Matter, and spoken out against homophobia, told a local Spanish magazine that he will shake President Donald Trump's hand today — but only under duress.

https://x.com/IrishStarUS/status/2078833043788169438

"I don't want to go to prison," Iglesias said. "I hope to greet him at a time when we are all very happy, and that it passes very quickly and I can forget about it."

Trump's Trophy Tradition

The US president is set to present the Jules Rimet trophy at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, where Argentina face Spain in the 2026 FIFA World Cup Final. It will be the second consecutive time Trump has handed out a major FIFA trophy on American soil, following his appearance at last year's revamped Club World Cup final.

That earlier ceremony left a lasting impression on Spain's squad — particularly on defender Marc Cucurella, who crossed paths with Trump when Chelsea won the competition.

"We were told that Trump would hand over the trophy, and that we couldn't lift it until he left. We were all standing there, waiting for him to go, but he just stood still. He said: 'Go on, lift it, I'll stay here.' I was absolutely terrified."

— Marc Cucurella, Spain and Chelsea defender

Cucurella, whose curly hair has become a trademark of this Spanish squad, told AS that Trump "wanted to be right there with us" during the celebration. The Chelsea full-back holds the unusual distinction of being the only Spanish athlete ever photographed with the president.

Politics Meets the Pitch

Iglesias was careful to frame his reluctance as pragmatic rather than confrontational. "I don't think this is the time to create controversy," he said. "People know perfectly well what I think. I would love to do many things, but the reality is that even if people think I am all-powerful, I don't have that much power to tackle certain things."

Trump has already injected himself into the tournament's narrative. Earlier in the competition, he publicly called for a review of a red card shown to US star Folarin Balogun — a request that was successful, drawing criticism from those who saw it as political interference in the sport.

The Stakes at MetLife

Today's final pits Lionel Messi's Argentina, seeking a third consecutive major trophy, against Spain, the reigning European champions who dismantled France in the semifinal. The match carries a record $50 million prize for the winner, with average ticket prices reportedly exceeding $11,000.

For the millions of Indian football fans who have followed this tournament from living rooms in New Jersey, Houston, and the Bay Area — and from couches in Mumbai and Delhi where restaurants stayed open past midnight — the final represents the culmination of a month-long global spectacle.

Whether the post-match trophy presentation will generate as many headlines as the match itself remains to be seen. Iglesias, at least, has already decided his approach: comply, and move on.
